title: Chunked Budget Allocation Prevents Non-Monotonic Regressions in World-Model Verification

contributions.purpose: Identifies why increasing verification budget can paradoxically reduce agent task success in sequential verify-and-retry.
contributions.mechanism: Names and characterizes trajectory drift: when the world model rejects a checkout (often a false negative), the agent re-browses and frequently selects a worse product than originally found.
contributions.evaluation: Trajectory drift accounts for 60.5% of failures when agents re-browse after verification rejection.
contributions.source_quote: We identify trajectory drift as the dominant failure mode in sequential verify-and-retry, accounting for 60.5% of failures when agents re-browse after verification rejection.

contributions.purpose: Prevents non-monotonic regressions by restructuring how a fixed verification budget is spent.
contributions.mechanism: Chunked budget allocation: instead of spreading budget B across many sequential cycles, allocate it across M cycles with K = B/M parallel world-model rollouts per cycle (M = 1 spends the whole budget in one parallel chunk).
contributions.evaluation: On WebShop, chunked verification (M = 1) achieves 21.50% task success versus 0.86% for sequential verify-and-retry (M = 10), a 25x improvement at the same budget.
contributions.source_quote: We demonstrate that chunked budget allocation achieves a 25x improvement in task success rate (21.50% vs. 0.86%) by eliminating sequential verification cycles.

contributions.purpose: Shows that sophisticated aggregation does not help when the world model is poorly calibrated.
contributions.mechanism: Compares consensus aggregation across parallel rollouts against single-rollout acceptance.
contributions.evaluation: Consensus provides no benefit because the world model predicts failure (p-hat = 0) for 98.4% of cycles, causing consensus to degenerate.
contributions.source_quote: We show that consensus aggregation across parallel rollouts provides no benefit over single-rollout acceptance, as the world model's poor calibration (predicting p-hat = 0 for 98.4% of cycles) causes consensus to degenerate.

contributions.purpose: Gives practitioners a concrete rule for spending verification budget.
contributions.mechanism: Ablation over the number of cycles M showing performance degrades monotonically as M increases.
contributions.evaluation: M = 1 (all budget in one parallel chunk) consistently outperforms finer-grained allocations.
contributions.source_quote: We provide practical guidance: setting M = 1 (spending all budget in one parallel chunk) consistently outperforms finer-grained allocations, with performance degrading monotonically as M increases.

self_declared_provenance.quote: Our work is complementary: rather than improving world model accuracy, we study how to allocate a fixed verification budget effectively.

Our findings reveal a surprising limitation: for verification of irreversible actions, the allocation structure (chunked vs. sequential) matters more than the aggregation rule (consensus vs. first-rollout).

However, these approaches assume that retry improves outcomes. We show that for irreversible actions, sequential retry can cause trajectory drift, where rejected checkouts trigger re-browsing that leads to worse product selections.

notes: Contains an embedded negative/null result: consensus aggregation provides no benefit over single-rollout acceptance (C3). Absolute success rates are low (21.50% best case); the 25x headline compares against a 0.86% degenerate baseline.
